title: Why McCoy's 1872 Patent Wasn't a Safety Valve
topic: Why the American inventor Elijah McCoy added a safety valve to his steam engine (Cleveland, 1872)

lines: McCoy oils railroad engines, then builds a machine to feed oil without stopping.
He works as a fireman and oiler at the Michigan Central Railroad.
McCoy can find only that work in Michigan.
Other automatic oilers have already been patented.
McCoy does skilled work in a home machine shop in Ypsilanti.
He keeps refining his devices.
A safety valve releases steam when pressure rises past a set limit.
Boilers without one can explode.
Firemen or crew members tie down valves for extra power.
Tying a valve down pushes pressure past the safe limit.
In 1872, McCoy patents his automatic lubricator for locomotives and ships.
He lacks the money to build lubricators in large numbers.
So McCoy assigns or sells his patent rights.
You see, it's like a water bottle in your bag, so you never stop.
His lubricator feeds oil to steam engines automatically.
Trains run faster and stop less for lubrication and maintenance.
The real reason: his 1872 patent is an automatic lubricator.
It oils the steam engines of locomotives and ships.
By 1899, his lubricator runs on almost all North American railroads.
But McCoy's 1872 patent is not a safety valve.
And 'the real McCoy' comes from Scotland, not from McCoy.

claims.claim: When Elijah McCoy arrived in Michigan, he could find work only as a fireman and oiler at the Michigan Central Railroad.
In a home-based machine shop in Ypsilanti, McCoy did more highly skilled work, such as developing improvements and inventions, and he continued to refine his devices and design new ones.
Similar automatic oilers had been patented previously.
A safety valve automatically releases a substance from a boiler, pressure vessel, or other system when the pressure or temperature exceeds preset limits.
Early boilers operating without safety valves were prone to explosion unless carefully operated.

Firemen or crew members tied down safety valves to increase the pressure and power of the engine, at further risk of explosion; spring valves could also be screwed down to increase pressure beyond design limits, a dangerous practice sometimes used to marginally increase steam engine performance.
McCoy invented an automatic lubricator for oiling the steam engines of locomotives and ships, patenting it in 1872 as 'Improvement in Lubricators for Steam-Engines' (U.S. patent 129,843).
Lacking the capital with which to manufacture his lubricators in large numbers, McCoy usually assigned his patent rights to his employers or sold them to investors.
Lubricators enabled trains to run faster and more profitably with less need to stop for lubrication and maintenance.
In 1899, the Michigan Bureau of Labor and Industrial Statistics reported that the McCoy lubricator was in use on almost all North American railroads.
The phrase 'the real McCoy' originates from Scotland and has nothing to do with Elijah McCoy.
